title: Extracted teeth, amalgam and dental clinical waste
audience: Cleaners and dental assistants who handle clinical waste, extracted teeth and imaging chemicals.
learningOutcomes: Separate medical waste from general waste at the point it is collected.
Handle a bag of clinical waste without compacting or overfilling it.
Choose the correct route for an extracted tooth, including one with a dental amalgam restoration.

instruction.heading: What counts as clinical waste
instruction.body: Clinical or medical waste from a dental practice includes recognisable human tissue, with teeth treated separately, and any material or solution that carries free-flowing blood. The rules that govern disposal are the state and territory regulations and the local environment authority's guidance, not one national rule. Separate waste at its origin into medical and non-medical streams, colour code and label medical waste, and use bags that meet the applicable clinical waste bag standard.

instruction.heading: Handling bags and containers
instruction.body: The usual barrier kit of gloves, a face mask and goggles applies whenever clinical waste is handled. Bags and boxes are not overfilled, and nothing is pressed down inside them. Clinical waste and sharps boxes wait in secure storage for a licensed contractor, who collects them for approved treatment. Chemical waste, including some dental chemicals and mercury, never goes to a landfill tip that compacts waste.

instruction.heading: Extracted teeth
instruction.body: Once an extracted tooth has been rinsed free of visible blood, grit, soft tissue and spit, it may be given back to the patient on request. Otherwise it could be enclosed in paper, or set in plaster inside a disposable cup, then put in ordinary rubbish under the local rule. Certain states and territories restrict burning teeth that carry dental amalgam, because mercury vapour is released, so those teeth must not go into medical waste or sharps containers. Check the local rule before disposing of any tooth.

instruction.heading: Chemical waste from imaging
instruction.body: Imaging chemicals and some disinfectants have their own disposal route. The source refers to a companion practice guide for the detail, which this lesson does not reproduce. Use the practice's documented chemical waste route, and never pour a chemical into a general drain unless the written plan allows it.

procedure: Separate medical waste from general waste at the point where you collect it.
Before lifting a bag, put on gloves, a face mask and goggles.
Fill bags only to the marked level, and never press a bag down by hand.
Seal the bag and move it to the secured store for licensed collection.
Check the local rule before disposing of an extracted tooth, especially one with amalgam.
Keep chemical waste out of medical bins and out of general waste.

workedExamples.situation: A medical waste bag is almost full, and someone is about to press it down by hand to fit one more item.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop. Replace the bag or seal it as it is. Do not compact it by hand. Move it to the storage point for licensed collection.

workedExamples.situation: A used extracted tooth with a silver-coloured filling is in a tray, and the nearest bin is labelled as medical waste.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not place a tooth with amalgam into medical waste or a sharps container. Check the local rule and the practice protocol before disposing of it, and ask the dental nurse.

equipmentAndPpe: Gloves, a face mask and goggles for handling waste
Leak-proof bags marked as biohazard, in the colour set by the local rule
Sharps containers held in secured storage

commonErrors.error: Compacting a bag by hand to make room.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not press bags down. Seal them at the marked level.

commonErrors.error: Putting an amalgam-restored tooth into the sharps container.
commonErrors.prevention: Follow the local rule for those teeth.

commonErrors.error: Tipping chemical waste into the general rubbish.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the documented chemical waste route.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Waste rules vary by state, territory and council. This lesson does not state a rule for any location.
Licensed contractors collect and treat clinical waste. This lesson does not grant a licence to collect, carry or treat waste.
Mercury and other chemical waste must not go to refuse tips that compact open landfill.
The source names Australian standards and state rules.

qualityStandard: No bag is compacted by hand.
No tooth or chemical is set on a route the local rule does not allow.
documentationEvidence: Waste collection record with date, container count and collector
Note of any unusual item, such as a tooth with amalgam, and the route used
summary: Separate waste at source, seal bags at the marked level, and never compact by hand.
Teeth with amalgam follow the local rule and never go into medical waste or sharps containers.
Chemical waste follows the documented route, and licensed collection is not done by the cleaner.

knowledgeChecks.question: A medical waste bag is nearly full. What is the correct action?
options: Compress it by hand to fit more in and tie the top very tightly.
Seal it without overfilling and move it to the store for licensed collection.
Overfill it and leave it on the floor by the door for the cleaner.
Put it in the general bin with the other waste from the room today.

knowledgeChecks.question: An extracted tooth has an amalgam filling. Which is correct?
options: Put it into a sharps box and send it to the sharps collector with the other bins today.
Follow the local rule set by the state or territory for that tooth, and do not assume it can be incinerated.
Flush it down the sink and rinse the sink with hot water and then wipe the whole bench down.
Put it in an open general bin in the staff room next to the kettle, the milk and the cups.

knowledgeChecks.question: Where do imaging chemicals go?
options: Into the general bin with the lid left open so the rest of the day's rubbish can go in too.
Down the drain whenever convenient and the drain is then flushed with hot water.
Through the practice's documented chemical waste route, and never to a compacting landfill tip.
Into the waste compactor at the back of the building with the general waste bag.

sourceReferences: ADA Guidelines for Infection Control, 3rd ed. (Australian Dental Association, 2015), section B.5 (management of clinical waste), including the notes on extracted teeth and chemical waste; rights: user-held; reworded (no copying)
